# Stanford University: Converting Monopoly into Permanence {#sec-2-12}

::: {.chapter-meta}
Act II — Land, Monopoly, and Institution · 1884–1893
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="draft"}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Pre-Draft Brief

**Core question.** How does power outlive its founders?

**The answer.** By buying an institution. A railroad fortune is a depreciating
asset with enemies; a university is a permanent one with admirers. The Founding
Grant of 1885 created a private institution with a self-perpetuating board,
insulated from electoral politics, endowed with land that could only appreciate.
Rail controlled movement. Stanford was built to control succession.

**The mechanism.** All three at once, which is why this chapter is the hinge of
the book. The endowment is monopoly rent (public subsidy, privately captured)
converted into an institution that reproduces an elite (network) and certifies
its authority (legitimacy chokepoint). The Medici altarpiece from Act I ch. 7,
at scale, with a charter.

**The key fact.** Leland Stanford Jr. died in Florence in March 1884, aged
fifteen. The Founding Grant was executed on 11 November 1885. The university
opened on 1 October 1891 on some eight thousand acres of the family's farm —
land that came from the railroad.

**The human anchor.** Stanford and his wife, after Florence, deciding that the
children of California shall be our children. Take the grief seriously. The
chapter is stronger if the motive is genuine, because the mechanism does not
require cynicism to operate.

**Excluded voices.** The Chinese labourers whose unpaid differential is inside
the endowment, the ranch workers on the farm the campus was built on, and the
Muwekma Ohlone whose land it was before either. Also everyone the new
institution's first president would shortly classify as unfit.

**Proof.** This chapter proves that monopoly rent converts into institutional
permanence by showing the specific legal instrument — a self-perpetuating board,
tax-advantaged, insulated from politics, endowed with appreciating land — that
made the conversion durable.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Working summary

Leland Stanford Jr. died of typhoid in Florence in March 1884, aged fifteen. The
Founding Grant that created a university in his name was executed on 11 November
1885, and Stanford University opened on 1 October 1891 on some eight thousand
acres of the family's Palo Alto farm — land that came from the railroad.

The chapter takes the grief seriously. The children of California shall be our
children is not a cynical sentence, and the argument does not require it to be
one. The mechanism operates whether or not the motive is sincere, which is
precisely what makes it a mechanism.

What the Founding Grant actually did is the chapter's substance, and it is a
legal document worth reading closely. It created a private institution governed
by a self-perpetuating board that replaced its own members, insulated from
electoral politics and from the legislature, endowed with land that could not be
sold and could therefore only appreciate. A railroad fortune is a depreciating
asset with enemies and regulators. A university is a permanent one with
admirers, and it produces people rather than merely distributing money.

The genuinely progressive features were real: free tuition, coeducation from the
first day, and a practical curriculum aimed at usefulness rather than
gentlemanly polish. They are also the legitimacy, and the chapter holds both
facts at once. The first president, David Starr Jordan, was a distinguished
biologist and one of the most prominent eugenicists in America — introduced
here, and taken up properly in Act III.

Six centuries earlier a Florentine banking family commissioned altarpieces for
the same reason. The structure is identical: private capital converting
accumulated rent into public meaning, permanently, with the donor's name
attached.

Inside that endowment sits the wage differential never paid to the Central
Pacific's Chinese workforce, the labour of the farm the campus replaced, and the
Muwekma Ohlone land beneath all of it.

Rail controlled movement. Stanford was built to control succession. Whether it
can do that without its founders is the next chapter.
:::

## Beats

1. **Hook.** Florence, March 1884. A fifteen-year-old dies of typhoid and a
   university is the consequence. Correct the date the drafts get wrong: 1884,
   not 1885.
2. **Grief as motive.** The children of California shall be our children. Do not
   undercut it. The argument does not need the motive to be false.
3. **The Founding Grant, 11 November 1885.** Read the instrument closely: what
   powers the trustees have, how they are replaced, what the endowment consists
   of.
4. **Why a university and not a foundation.** Legitimacy, permanence, and the
   specific advantage of an institution that produces people rather than grants.
5. **The land.** Eight thousand acres of the Palo Alto farm. Where it came from.
   The university is a railroad asset with a curriculum.
6. **Opening, 1 October 1891.** Free tuition, coeducation, and the practical
   curriculum. State the genuinely progressive features; they are real, and they
   are also the legitimacy.
7. **David Starr Jordan.** The first president: a biologist and a leading
   eugenicist. Introduce, do not resolve — ch. 3 of Act III does the work.
8. **The Medici callback.** One paragraph. Private capital commissioning public
   meaning, six centuries apart, same structure.
9. **The excluded.** Chinese labour inside the endowment; farm workers; Muwekma
   Ohlone land.
10. **Landing.** The sentence the book has been building to: rail controlled
   movement, Stanford controls succession. Then hand to ch. 13 — can it survive
   its founders?

:::

::: {.chapter-question}
How does power outlive its founders?
:::

Leland Stanford Jr. died of typhoid fever in Florence on 13 March 1884, two
months short of his sixteenth birthday. He was the Stanfords' only child. They
had been travelling in Europe, as they often did, and he had been collecting
antiquities with the seriousness of a boy who intended to have a museum.

His father is supposed to have said, on recovering from the collapse that
followed, that the children of California would be their children.

Twenty months later, on 11 November 1885, Leland and Jane Stanford executed the
Founding Grant of the Leland Stanford Junior University. It opened on 1 October
1891 on some eight thousand acres of the family's Palo Alto farm.

## Take the grief seriously

There is a cynical version of this chapter available and it is the wrong one.

The grief was real, and the family's response to it was consistent with how they
had behaved before. Stanford had been a trustee of other institutions. Jane
Stanford's involvement in the university over the following two decades was
sustained, detailed, and personally costly in a way that no public-relations
motive would explain.

The argument of this book does not require the motive to be false. It requires
only that the mechanism operate, and mechanisms do not care about intentions. A
sincere man converting a monopoly fortune into a permanent institution produces
the same structure as a calculating one, which is precisely what makes it a
mechanism rather than a scheme.

## What the instrument actually did

The Founding Grant is a legal document and it repays close reading, because
almost every feature that makes Stanford what it is was decided in it.

It created a private corporation governed by a board of trustees. The trustees,
after the founders' deaths, would fill their own vacancies. There is no
electorate, no legislative oversight, and no external appointing authority. The
board is self-perpetuating, which means the institution's governance is
insulated from politics permanently and by design.

It endowed the university with land — the Palo Alto farm, together with holdings
elsewhere in California — and it directed that the land not be sold. Income was
to come from its use, not its disposal.

That prohibition is the single most consequential clause in the document, and
its consequences would not be visible for sixty-six years. A university that
cannot sell its land can only lease it, and in 1951 a dean of engineering will
notice that leasing eight thousand acres of the San Francisco Peninsula to
technology companies is an extraordinarily good business. Act IV opens on it.

The Grant also specified the university's purposes in broad terms, provided for
coeducation, and directed that tuition be free — which it was for the first
several decades.

## Why a university

Consider the alternatives available to a man in Stanford's position in 1885.

He could leave the money to heirs. He had no heir. He could leave it as a
foundation making grants, though the modern grant-making foundation barely
existed yet. He could endow a hospital, a library, a museum — all of which he
and his wife also did, at smaller scale.

A railroad fortune, meanwhile, was a depreciating political asset. The Southern
Pacific was the most detested institution in California. It was subject to a
constitutional convention called largely to control it, to a federal government
that would shortly sue his estate, and to continuous public hostility. Anything
directly attached to it was contestable.

A university is different in kind. It is permanent, it is admired, it is
extremely difficult to tax or regulate, and its output is people. An institution
that produces the next generation's lawyers, engineers, and administrators
acquires a form of influence that does not appear on any balance sheet and
cannot be broken up by an antitrust action.

Six hundred years earlier a Florentine banking family had reached the same
conclusion about altarpieces, for the same reason: private capital converting
accumulated rent into public meaning, permanently, with the donor's name on it.
Act I chapter 7 described the transaction. This is the same transaction at
industrial scale, and the name is on the institution rather than on a painting.

## The genuinely admirable parts

The chapter has to hold two things at once here, and the way to do it is to
state both without hedging.

The university that opened in 1891 was, in several respects, more progressive
than its eastern models. It was coeducational from the first day, when most
elite American institutions were not. Tuition was free. The curriculum was
practical and elective rather than a fixed classical course, and engineering and
the sciences were central rather than peripheral. It admitted students without
regard to religious affiliation, and it was non-denominational at a time when
that was unusual.

Those features are real and they benefited a great many people. They are also
the legitimacy, and the two facts do not cancel.

## Jordan

The first president was David Starr Jordan, an ichthyologist recruited from
Indiana University, thirty-nine years old and already among the most prominent
scientists in the country.

He was also, by the turn of the century, one of the most prominent eugenicists
in the United States — chairman of the eugenics committee of the American
Breeders Association, an advocate of sterilisation legislation, and the author
of works arguing that human quality was hereditary and that social policy should
act on the fact.

Act III chapter 3 takes this up properly and this chapter does not resolve it.
What matters here is the sequence: the institution built to reproduce
California's elite selected as its first head a man whose scientific work was
about which people should reproduce.

## The horses, and a bet about photography

There is one more thing on the farm worth recording, because it is the most
frequently repeated Stanford anecdote and it is usually told wrong.

Stanford bred and raced trotting horses at Palo Alto, seriously and at
considerable expense, and he wanted to know whether a trotting horse ever has
all four feet off the ground at once. In the 1870s he engaged the photographer
Eadweard Muybridge to find out. Muybridge eventually rigged a line of cameras
triggered in sequence by the horse itself, and in 1878 produced the sequential
photographs that answered the question. The horse does leave the ground.

The standard version has this inventing cinema. It did not. Motion photography
developed from many directions over the following two decades, and Muybridge's
sequences were one contributing line among several. The claim is frequently
overstated and this book will not repeat it.

What the episode does demonstrate is something the rest of the chapter is about.
A private fortune of sufficient size can commission the answer to a question
nobody else has the resources to ask, and the resulting knowledge carries the
patron's name and serves his interest — in this case a stock farm, a scientific
curiosity, and a reputation for enlightened patronage. Muybridge did the work.
Stanford paid, took the credit in the resulting publication, and the two of them
fell out over it.

That is the Medici transaction again, in a paddock, with cameras. And the
university is the same transaction with a charter.

## What is inside the endowment

The eight thousand acres came from the farm. The farm and the fortune came from
the railroad. The railroad was built with federal land grants, federal bonds,
and a workforce paid a differential that was never made up.

Inside the endowment of Stanford University, in a precise and traceable sense,
sits the money that was not paid to the men who drove the Summit Tunnel.

Beneath it is land that was a Mexican rancho, and before that was the territory
of the Muwekma Ohlone, who appear in the mission registers of chapter 1 and in
the Founding Grant not at all.

## The sentence

Rail controlled movement. Stanford was built to control succession.

That is the transaction: an extractive fortune, held in a form that was
politically vulnerable and legally exposed, converted into an institution that
is neither — governed by a board that appoints itself, funded by land that
cannot be sold, and producing, indefinitely, the people who will run the state.

Whether it could survive its founders was not yet established. Within eight
years both of them would be dead, the estate would be frozen, the federal
government would be suing for fifteen million dollars, and the university would
nearly close.
